title: Use of the Content-Disposition Header Field in the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP)
summary: RFC 2616 mentioned Content-Disposition but said it was not part of HTTP/1.1. This standards-track document takes over its definition for HTTP and clarifies internationalization. It is the header used to suggest file names for downloads.

plainLanguage.summary: A server can say save this as a file with this name. This writes down exactly how to say that, including names with accents.

questions: how to suggest download filename in http
how to set download filename in http
what is the difference between inline and attachment
subtitle: The HTTP header that tells a browser to save a response as a file, and what name to give it.

tldr.problem: RFC 2616 described Content-Disposition but said it was not part of HTTP/1.1, and implementations disagreed about how to handle file names with non-ASCII characters.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6266 defines a profile of the MIME header for HTTP, with the disposition types inline and attachment and a filename parameter, plus a filename* parameter that uses the RFC 5987 encoding for international characters.
tldr.outcome: Servers can suggest download names reliably, and recipients are told to treat the name as advisory only. RFC 6266 updates RFC 2616 and is a Standards Track document.

facts.label: Disposition types
facts.value: inline, attachment, or an extension token

today: RFC 6266 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2011 that updates RFC 2616, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its Appendix D notes that its advice reflects user agent behavior at the time of writing and might be superseded.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2616 defines the Content-Disposition response header field but points out that it is not part of the HTTP/1.1 Standard, only documented because it is widely implemented. RFC 6266 takes over its definition and registration as used in HTTP.

Based on interoperability testing with existing user agents, it fully defines a profile of the features in the MIME variant (RFC 2183) of the header field, and it clarifies internationalization. It does not apply to Content-Disposition fields inside payload bodies, such as in multipart/form-data.
sections.plainLanguage: Browsers already used this label for downloads, but nobody had written the rules down properly. This document does that.

sections.title: Conformance and Error Handling
sections.content:
The specification sets rules for senders, usually HTTP origin servers, and recipients, usually user agents. Senders MUST NOT generate invalid Content-Disposition fields.

Recipients MAY try to recover a usable value from an invalid field, but SHOULD NOT reject the message outright unless that is desirable, for example in a validator. The default handling of an invalid field is to ignore it.
sections.plainLanguage: If the label is written wrongly, the browser should not refuse the whole parcel. It can just ignore the label.

sections.title: The Header Field
sections.content:
The header conveys how to process the response payload and can carry metadata such as the file name to use when saving. Its value is a disposition type followed by zero or more parameters separated by semicolons.

The type is inline, attachment or an extension token, matched case-insensitively. attachment tells the recipient to prompt the user to save the response locally rather than process it normally. inline means default processing, so it is only useful when combined with parameters such as a file name. Unknown types SHOULD be handled like attachment.

Multiple instances of the same parameter name make the value invalid. Recipients SHOULD ignore unrecognized parameters, which allows future extension. The registry for types and parameters is the one from RFC 2183, shared with MIME, so not every registered value makes sense in HTTP.
sections.plainLanguage: The label says either show it now or save it. Anything the browser does not understand is treated as save it.

sections.title: File Names and International Characters
sections.content:
Two parameters carry the suggested file name. filename uses a plain value, which cannot hold characters outside ISO-8859-1. filename* uses the encoding from RFC 5987, which allows other characters and an optional language tag. The two differ only in that encoding.

Many older user agents do not understand filename*. So when both are present, recipients SHOULD pick filename* and ignore filename. Senders can therefore send both and avoid special-casing particular user agents.

Appendix C explains why other approaches are worse: RFC 2047 encoded words are not meant for parameters, percent encoding depends on the guessed character set, and encoding sniffing is not interoperable and risks misreading the value.
sections.plainLanguage: One note spells the name with plain letters for old programs. The other spells it with fancy letters for newer ones, and newer ones should read the fancy one.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives four examples. An attachment with filename=example.html shows a save-as dialog. An INLINE value with a quoted name an example.html behaves as if there were no header but remembers the name for a later save. The quoted form is used here so the name can contain a space.

A filename* value of UTF-8''%e2%82%ac%20rates encodes the euro sign (U+20AC) followed by a space and the word rates. The last example adds filename="EURO rates" before it as a fallback for user agents that do not implement RFC 5987.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show the same parcel label written for old and new programs, with and without a euro sign in the name.

sections.title: Safe Handling of Filenames
sections.content:
Building a local file name from server-provided information is risky, so the RFC treats the name as advisory only. Recipients MUST NOT be able to write outside locations they are entitled to. One strategy is to strip all but the last path segment, where segments are delimited by \ and /.

Because many platforms rely on file extensions for type information, trusting the server's extension could cause privilege escalation, for instance with .exe. Recipients that use extensions MUST ensure a safe one is used, ideally matching the media type.

Recipients SHOULD also strip or replace control characters and leading or trailing whitespace, and SHOULD ignore or substitute names with special meaning such as ., .., ~, | and device names.
sections.plainLanguage: A website must not be allowed to choose where on your computer a file goes or to sneak a dangerous file type past you. The browser has to treat the suggested name as only a suggestion.
